title: Best Multi-Cloud Cost Management Tools for AWS, GCP, and Azure
summary: Compare Pump, Vantage, Finout, CloudZero, DoiT, nOps, and native AWS, GCP, and Azure tools on allocation, forecasting, anomaly alerts, automated savings, and pricing.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


-


Choose a multi-cloud cost management tool based on your cloud mix, your allocation needs, and whether you want the tool to recommend savings or carry them out for you.


-


Start with[Pump](https://www.pump.co/) if you want AWS, GCP, and Azure visibility and executed savings from one platform. Pump View is free for all three clouds, and Pump Save buys and manages commitments on your behalf, with no platform fee and no share of savings.


-


Native AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure tools can cover you if you use one provider and only need basic cost reporting. None of them reports across clouds.


-


Consider Finout or CloudZero for complex shared-cost allocation and unit economics, DoiT if you want managed FinOps advisory, and nOps if your commitment work is AWS-only and you accept share-of-savings pricing.


-


Use the comparison table below to check what each tool supports. Its entries draw on primary vendor documentation and mark unconfirmed capabilities.

## How to evaluate a multi-cloud cost tool


A tool can support AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure without offering the same capabilities for each provider. Check provider coverage separately for cost allocation, forecasts, anomaly alerts, and savings actions. A three-cloud logo alone does not tell you which features work across your cloud mix.


Allocation requires more scrutiny than a tagging checkbox. The[FinOps Foundation’s allocation guidance](https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation/) covers direct costs and shared costs assigned through accounts, tags, labels, or derived metadata. Ask how a tool divides a shared database bill among products and where it puts charges it cannot assign. A fixed-percentage split can produce different product costs than a split based on usage.


Forecasts need a stated basis. The[FinOps Foundation’s forecasting guidance](https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/forecasting/) accounts for historical usage, planned changes, pricing, discounts, and business drivers. Ask whether the tool extends a spending trend or incorporates a planned migration or contract change. For anomalies, check when the provider supplies billing data, how often the tool checks it, and who receives alerts. Frequent checks cannot reveal a charge before the provider reports it.


Finally, distinguish savings advice from action. A recommendation leaves implementation with you, while automated commitment purchases or infrastructure changes require permission and approval controls. Ask whether onboarding needs read-only billing access, an installed agent, or write permissions. Compare subscription fees, tracked-spend limits, savings-based charges, and underlying billing-export fees against your expected usage.


## Pump: free multi-cloud visibility plus savings Pump executes for you


Pump fits you when you want AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure spend in one place and want the savings work done rather than handed back to you as a to-do list.[Pump View](https://www.pump.co/view) brings AWS, GCP, Azure, and more than 20 engineering tools into a single dashboard, where you can set budgets, forecast spend, build and schedule custom reports, and receive automatic anomaly alerts in Slack, email, or text. View also explains why your spend changed, not just that it changed. Setup takes under five minutes with a read-only permission, and dashboards populate in minutes.


[Pump Save](https://www.pump.co/save) handles execution. Pump buys and manages long-term commitments across AWS, GCP, and Azure on your behalf, then shifts them as your usage changes so you get the discount without the lock-in risk. It also delivers rightsizing recommendations from continuous analysis of CPU, memory, and traffic patterns. Pump reports that more than 3,000 engineering teams use it to cut cloud costs 20% to 30%, and that most customers see savings within the first week. Kubernetes and Spot autoscaling are on the roadmap and labeled coming soon, so plan around commitment management and rightsizing today.


Pricing is the clearest difference from the rest of this list. Pump’s Cloud plan is[$0 per year](https://www.pump.co/pricing) with no platform fee and no percentage of savings, because cloud providers pay Pump to manage billing complexity. The plan includes cost allocation tagging that assigns nearly 100% of spend, budgets, forecasts, anomaly detection, custom cost queries, scheduled reports, and task assignment to Linear or Slack. A Custom plan adds bring-your-own-cloud root management, advanced security, automated penetration testing, two-year data retention, and a dedicated support team at a quoted price. There is no tracked-spend cap, annual platform fee, or share-of-savings charge to model.


## Vantage: broad multi-cloud and AI/SaaS cost visibility


Vantage fits you if your AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure bills sit alongside AI or SaaS spending. Its[integrations and virtual tagging](https://www.vantage.sh/) let you group costs without changing tags in each provider. Vantage also lists unit costs, budgets, anomaly alerts, and Kubernetes rightsizing, though its product page does not establish equal feature depth across providers.


Vantage’s automation covers less than its reporting. Autopilot manages AWS Savings Plans, but Vantage does not document Autopilot for Google Cloud or Azure. If you need automated savings actions across all three clouds, verify what Vantage can do for each provider.


The[Starter plan](https://www.vantage.sh/pricing) is free for up to $2,500 in tracked cloud spend. Pro costs $30 per month for up to $7,500, Business costs $200 per month for up to $20,000, and Enterprise uses custom pricing. Virtual tagging appears on paid plan cards, but the pricing page does not clearly establish which tier includes every listed capability.


## Finout: shared-cost allocation and unit economics at scale


Finout suits you when cloud costs need to be assigned to customers, tenants, or products, especially when several share the same infrastructure. Its[virtual tags and shared-cost allocation tools](https://www.finout.io/) let you group charges without relying only on provider tags. Finout also reports unit costs, such as spend per customer, across connected sources that include AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, OCI, and Kubernetes.


For optimization, Finout says its orchestration agent proposes actions such as rightsizing and idle-resource cleanup. The agent routes proposed changes through existing approval flows, and you can opt in to automatic application for individual workflows. Finout also claims you can see an initial anomaly or unit-cost view within 48 hours and complete multicloud allocation and chargeback within two weeks. Treat those as vendor targets, not guaranteed onboarding times.


Finout offers a free trial, but[paid pricing](https://www.finout.io/pricing) requires a quote for a fixed annual fee based on committed cloud and AI spend and complexity. That model may fit if detailed chargeback justifies a platform budget. Confirm connector permissions and the quoted cost before committing.


## CloudZero: unit cost and AI ROI focus


CloudZero suits you when your main question is what each customer, product, or feature costs to serve, rather than what your cloud accounts spend in total. Its[platform](https://www.cloudzero.com/) connects AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, and AI and SaaS cost sources. CloudZero can allocate shared spend across business dimensions, giving you a cost basis for assessing customer margins or AI feature economics.


CloudZero’s[pricing page](https://www.cloudzero.com/pricing/) lists forecasts, anomaly detection, and optimization recommendations under a single subscription. The subscription includes unlimited cost sources, users, dimensions, and dashboards, but pricing requires a custom quote based on scale and complexity. CloudZero documents savings recommendations, not automatic infrastructure changes, so you would need a way to review and carry out those actions.


## DoiT: tagless allocation with managed FinOps support


DoiT suits organizations that want cost allocation across AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure alongside FinOps advisory support. Its[Cloud Intelligence platform](https://www.doit.com/) includes cost analysis, customer and team allocation, anomaly detection, and unit economics. DoiT advertises tagless allocation, but its claim that customers can allocate all spend from day one is a vendor claim, not a general guarantee.


Runtime-level attribution requires a billing integration and an eBPF sensor installed through Helm. Buyers evaluating tenant-level allocation should account for that installation rather than assuming DoiT works entirely from billing data. The[pricing page](https://www.doit.com/pricing/) lists Cloud Intelligence Essentials as free, while Enhanced and Enterprise use bespoke pricing. Real-time anomaly detection appears under Enhanced. PerfectScale commitment automation for AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure also carries provider-specific bespoke pricing, so the free tier should not be treated as including those paid capabilities or Attribute’s tiered offerings.


## nOps: AWS-heavy commitment optimization


nOps fits AWS-heavy organizations that want to optimize commitment rates as well as track costs. Its[AWS rate optimization documentation](https://www.nops.io/aws-rate-optimization/) describes showback and chargeback by account, tag, and business unit. That gives AWS buyers a clearer picture of its allocation methods than the available documentation gives buyers evaluating Google Cloud or Azure.


The[nOps pricing page](https://www.nops.io/pricing/) advertises hourly multi-cloud cost visibility and allocation, anomaly detection, and autonomous rate optimization across AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure. It does not establish that allocation and automation work to the same depth on each provider. The page explains AWS account connection and an optional agent, but buyers should confirm Google Cloud and Azure onboarding before committing. nOps charges a fixed fee based on cloud spend for visibility and allocation, while rate optimization costs a percentage of realized savings.


## Native AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure cost tools


If most of your spend sits with one provider, its native tools can answer cost questions without another cost-management platform.[AWS Cost Explorer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/ce-what-is.html) groups AWS costs and usage, forecasts up to 18 months, and offers Reserved Instance recommendations. Its console is free, while API requests cost $0.01 per paginated request. After you enable it, current-month data typically appears in about 24 hours, and AWS refreshes the data at least every 24 hours, subject to upstream delays.


[AWS Cost Anomaly Detection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/manage-ad.html) checks billing data about three times daily and can alert you by email or SNS. Detection may take up to 24 hours after usage occurs, so you should not treat its alerts as real-time. AWS identifies possible spending drivers, but its recommendations do not automatically change resources.


For Azure-first spending,[Microsoft Cost Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/overview-cost-management) provides cost analysis, exports, tag-based allocation, shared-cost splitting rules, budgets, and forecast alerts. Its subscription-level anomaly detection runs daily. Azure Advisor offers optimization recommendations, but those recommendations do not execute themselves.


For Google Cloud,[Cloud Billing](https://cloud.google.com/cost-management) provides console reports with forecasts up to 12 months, budgets with email or Pub/Sub alerts, and[Cost Anomaly Detection](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/cost-management/announcing-ga-of-cost-anomaly-detection/) that is on by default and monitors spend hourly. Detailed analysis requires enabling billing export to BigQuery, which carries standard BigQuery storage and query charges. Active Assist recommendations are applied manually. None of the three native tools gives you a unified view of AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure spending, which is the gap a multi-cloud platform fills.


## Which tool fits your cloud mix and FinOps stage


Start with Pump if you run on more than one cloud, or expect to, and want visibility and savings from one platform at no cost.[Pump View](https://www.pump.co/view) covers AWS, GCP, and Azure plus 20+ engineering tools on a[$0 plan](https://www.pump.co/pricing) , and[Pump Save](https://www.pump.co/save) buys and manages commitments across those providers on your behalf. Because cloud providers pay Pump, there is no tracked-spend cap, platform fee, or share of savings to budget for. Connect read-only access, see your savings estimate, and decide from your own billing data.


If you use one cloud and mainly need to track spending against budgets, that provider’s native cost tools may be enough. Add a platform when you need reporting across providers, deeper allocation, or someone to act on the savings the native tools only recommend.


Finout or DoiT deserves closer evaluation when shared infrastructure makes chargeback difficult. For example, if several customers use the same cluster, account tags may not tell you what each customer costs. Ask each vendor how it assigns those charges and handles spend it cannot allocate. The[FinOps Foundation’s allocation guidance](https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation/) distinguishes shared-cost methods from direct assignment by tags and accounts.


If AWS commitments drive most of your savings work, evaluate nOps for that specific job. Check its documented coverage before assuming the same allocation or automation depth applies to GCP and Azure.


## FAQs


-


**What counts as multi-cloud cost visibility?** A tool should bring AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure charges into one reporting view and let you see which accounts, services, or business units incurred them. Check provider coverage for each feature, since a shared dashboard does not guarantee shared forecasting or alerts.


-


**How does shared-cost allocation differ from tagging?** Tags identify charges that belong to a project or owner.[Shared-cost allocation](https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation/) divides charges that several groups use, such as a shared database, according to an agreed method. Ask how the tool assigns untagged charges.


-


**How often do anomaly alerts run?** Cadence varies.[AWS Cost Anomaly Detection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/manage-ad.html) checks billing data about three times daily, and detection can take up to 24 hours after use.[Microsoft Cost Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/overview-cost-management) detects subscription-level anomalies daily. Confirm Google Cloud’s cadence in current documentation before relying on it, and ask third-party vendors whether alerts wait for billing exports.


-


**Is Pump really free?** Yes. Pump’s Cloud plan is[$0 per year](https://www.pump.co/pricing) with no platform fee and no percentage of savings, because cloud providers pay Pump to manage billing complexity. Custom and Enterprise plans that add bring-your-own-cloud controls and dedicated support are quoted separately.


-


**Does Pump recommend savings or carry them out?** Both.[Pump Save](https://www.pump.co/save) buys and manages commitments across AWS, GCP, and Azure on your behalf and shifts them as usage changes. Rightsizing arrives as recommendations, and Kubernetes and Spot autoscaling are labeled coming soon.


-


**Are native tools enough for multi-cloud reporting?** Native tools can suit a single-cloud account, but AWS Cost Explorer reports AWS costs and Microsoft Cost Management reports Microsoft Cloud costs. You need another reporting layer to combine those bills with Google Cloud charges.


## Conclusion


Choose a multi-cloud cost management tool based on your cloud mix and FinOps maturity, not the length of its feature list. Native tools may be enough if you use one provider. If you need deep shared-cost allocation or managed advisory, compare Finout, CloudZero, or DoiT against those needs. If you want free visibility across AWS, GCP, and Azure and want commitments managed for you with no platform fee or share of savings, start with[Pump](https://www.pump.co/) . Connect read-only access, see your savings estimate, and decide from your own billing data.
